attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, stated as fact.

semantics.note: The universal negative ('not a single company') is kept. The bottom-line, spend-versus-return framing is compressed but not distorted.

contract.note: The plain reading requires a public, quantified pairing of AI spend and realised return. That follows the 'spent this much / got this' wording and is an ordinary reading. Whether a value figure with no matching spend counts decides the result.

evidence.note: Lloyds disclosed about £50m of Gen AI value in 2025, before the post. It gives no matching spend, so it does not meet the spend-and-return test. It does weigh against the breadth of the claim.
An anonymous survey executive says benefits exceeded costs. The company is unnamed and no figures are shown, so this cannot count as a counterexample under the contract.

reviews.rationale: The claim says no company has ever done this. Failing to find a counterexample does not prove that. The closest candidates (Lloyds' value figure, an anonymous Deloitte quote) do not pair spend with realised return, so they do not contradict it. The packet settles neither way.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion. 'As I've discussed previously' refers back to his own earlier writing.

semantics.note: All three clauses and the 'millions of dollars on tokens' scope are kept. The claim is sweeping and partly hyperbolic, but it is still a factual assertion.

contract.note: Several readings come from the evaluator: 'experimenting' as having no financially evaluated deployment, cost meaning prospective task cost, and a Q1 2026 window. These are reasonable and ordinary. Separating token metering from total-cost forecasting is fair to the speaker's words.

evidence.note: AWS's own product documentation shows token metering and budget caps. That measures costs already incurred. It does not show reliable forecasting of prospective costs or any enterprise's ROI.
AI Sweden's ROI calculator is a scenario tool with uncertain inputs. It is not a documented enterprise deployment with token spend and attributable returns.

reviews.rationale: Neither item meets the contradiction condition. There is no qualifying enterprise with documented spend and returns, and no demonstrated method for forecasting deployment costs. There is also no representative evidence that every qualifying buyer was only experimenting. The packet settles neither side.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The compound claim is kept whole: the accounting exception, the 50% share, and the named funders. The 'no path' and 'co-conspirators' parts are largely rhetorical and hard to operationalise.

contract.note: The speaker says 'now make up', at May 26. Pinning the backlog share to Q1 2026 and treating May snapshots as context only cuts against the speaker. A pre-publication May figure is the natural measure of 'now'. Reading 'upcoming revenues' as backlog is fair.

evidence.note: A secondary summary, dated May 6, reports Anthropic and OpenAI at 50%+ of about $2T in cloud backlogs. That fits the 50% part under a fair 'now' reading. Under the contract's Q1 window it is context only.
Anthropic's own disclosure of Amazon's investment shows that outside financing was received. It does not show that payments depend solely on such financing, or that no sustainable path exists.

reviews.rationale: Only the 50% backlog part has support, and that comes from a secondary May estimate the contract treats as context. Nothing in the packet tests the 'no path' and 'only way to pay' parts. Nothing contradicts any part. The contract's Q1 window is unfair to 'now', but fixing it would still leave the compound claim unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own generalisation in his own post.

semantics.note: The scope (customers burning millions in tokens) and both clauses are kept. 'Every story... comes back to' is partly rhetorical framing.

contract.note: Reading cost as total AI cost relative to returns, and sustainability as being justified by attributable benefit, is ordinary in context. The clause saying a missing accounting basis bars any verdict is an odd extra. It makes no difference here.

evidence.note: Business Insider reports that Uber's COO finds AI costs hard to justify. That is one customer's view with no figures, and it cannot establish a claim about the whole population.
Anthropic's own disclosure counts over 1,000 customers spending more than $1M annualised, so billing is visible. It says nothing about customers' total costs or returns in May.
A vendor claims $20M a year in savings for an unnamed customer. The token bill and the net calculation are missing. This is opposing context, not a counterexample.

reviews.rationale: No qualifying customer documents total costs and returns either way. Uber's case alone cannot show the generalisation, and the vendor and Anthropic disclosures do not contradict it under the contract. The evidence by the cutoff does not settle the claim.
